newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua, facing election, trapped in violent past.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua, facing election, trapped in violent past.

text.p: Nicaraguans vote to elect a new president on Sunday, faced with the choice of reinstating former left-wing Sandinista rulers or opting for a right-wing tainted by charges of a dictatorial past.

In a tight race, polls suggest that Arnoldo Aleman, the burly 50-year-old former mayor of Managua, may have the edge over his rival, former guerrilla commander Daniel Ortega, who headed Nicaragua's Marxist government from 1979 to 1990.
World attention has focused on Nicaragua's landmark elections, which will mark the first time in its battle-scarred history that a civilian, elected president hands over power to another.

Among those arriving on Friday to observe the vote are former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker and Organisation of American States chief Cesar Gaviria, the former president of Colombia.

Ortega, 50, has managed to narrow Aleman's once-hefty lead, preaching a message of reconciliation, and acknowledging his blunders in the 1980s when he fought an eight-year war with U.S.-backed Contra rebels and confiscated private property.

"Yes, we made mistakes in the past, but these mistakes will not be repeated," Ortega said in the festival-like atmosphere of his final campaign rally late on Wednesday in which he embraced his old enemies, the Contras, as brothers.
"We must learn to forgive in Nicaragua," he said. "The moment has arrived for peace, reconciliation and love."

Ortega has shed the military fatigues and communist dogma that made him the enemy of the United States in the 1980s, and tried to transform his party from fiery revolutionaries into a moderate social democratic party that respects the free market and private property.

But Aleman, a fierce anti-Sandinista who was jailed by Ortega's government in the 1980s, has called their conversion "a sham," and said a Sandinista victory would return Nicaragua to the "dark night" of its violent past.

"It doesn't matter if they offer the olive branch of peace, of honesty, of respect for private property and freedom if they are hiding the AK-47 rifle that imposes war. They are the same," Aleman told foreign correspondents on Thursday.
Ortega in turn has tried to equate an Aleman victory to a return of Anastasio Somoza, the right-wing dictator toppled by the Sandinista revolution in 1979 after decades of oppression.
While Aleman denies he had ties with pro-Somoza groups as a youth before the revolution, he admits that his father and brother did.
The open hostility between the candidates has fuelled fears of renewed polarisation in Nicaragua, which was torn apart by an eight-year civil war in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead.

There are 21 other candidates in the presidential race, but they draw only a tiny fraction of the vote in public-opinion polls, reflecting the absence of a political centre in a country still caught in the divisions of the Cold War.
The latest CID-Gallup poll has Aleman's Liberal Alliance with 40.5 percent of the vote and Ortega close behind with 37.9 percent.
Aleman has tried to form a coalition bringing together Nicaragua's anti-Sandinista forces, warning that a vote for any other party is a vote for the Sandinistas.
Ortega said a vote for another party is a vote for Somoza.
This has put the squeeze on Nicaragua's other parties, preventing the emergence of a third, centrist option.

Another group in fear are Nicaragua's businesspeople, who have warned of dire economic consequences if Ortega wins. But in one of the poorest countries in the Western hemisphere, where more than half the population is unemployed or underemployed, Ortega's left-wing roots have continued to strike a chord with the poor.
